newsitem.title: UK: Resign call to minister in N. Irish jobs row. [CORRECTED 23:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Resign call to minister in N. Irish jobs row. [CORRECTED 23:00 GMT]

text.p: Leaders of minority Catholics called for the resignation of a key British minister for Northern Ireland on Sunday in a deepening row about her handling of measures to combat religious bias in employment.

But Baroness Jean Denton, the province's economy minister, who has been embroiled in week-long controversy about the transfer from her private office of a Catholic employee who suffered sectarian harassment, declared she would not quit.
A spokesman for Denton, who oversees British measures to outlaw job discrimination based on religion in the largely Protestant province, said the minister had "no intention of resigning".

Nationalist politicians, whose male Catholic constitutents have been shown by official figures to be 2.1 times more likely than Protestants to be unemployed, accused Denton of ignoring a code laid down by Britain to ease imbalances in the workforce.
(Corrects to insert word male and corrects figure to 2.1 from 2.5.)

Sinn Fein, the political arm of the banned Irish Republican Army, said its chairman Mitchel McLaughlin would raise concerns with U.S. politicians during a visit this week to Washington and New York, where Denton has been a frequent visitor to drum up investment in Northern Ireland.
Seamus Mallon, deputy leader of the moderate nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party, complained Denton and her officials had treated fair employment procedures with contempt.

"In these circumstances, the baroness's position as a minister is untenable and she should resign," he told Reuters. Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams echoed the call, saying new laws were needed to attack "the structured political discrimination" of Northern Ireland where Protestants support rule from Britain and Catholics want an all-Ireland state.

Denton told newspapers last week that she had suggested the Catholic official be given an alternative position two years ago because she as minister was "concerned about operational difficulties" affecting the efficiency of her private office.
Denton denied that the transfer was on sectarian grounds or linked to a religious harassment complaint by the official, her diary secretary, against the minister's private secretary.

"I was wholly unaware of any issues of a sectarian nature having arisen in my private office until informed of them subsequent to the move being made," Denton told the Irish News newspaper in Belfast.

Newspapers last week reported that while the victim, who subsequently received a 10,000 pound settlement and an apology from the Department of Agriculture, was transferred, the harasser was retained in her post although reprimanded.
According to the province's fair employment procedures, the victimiser, not the victim, should be transferred, the newspaper reports said.

In a second, unrelated controversy, BBC radio reported on Sunday that Denton had "sought and got" the appointment of a person who had not been shortlisted for a job as her "travelling secretary" in the Department of Economic Development.

"While this is not illegal it is contrary to the Fair Employment Code of Practice and while no discrimination is suggested in this case, authoratitive sources say that the way it was handled would make the appointment hard to defend if it were challenged on grounds of religious discrimination," BBC Northern Ireland's industry editor James Kerr, reported.

Denton's spokesman said the official, her Belfast-based departmental private secretary, had been off duty when the vacancy had been notified. No formal complaint had been made and and "therefore we don't feel that any action is necessary".
